correct_citation: Nickow, A., Oreopoulos, P., & Quan, V. (2020). The Impressive Effects of Tutoring on PreK-12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence. NBER Working Paper 27476. Published as Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan (2024), The Promise of Tutoring for PreK-12 Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence, American Educational Research Journal, doi:10.3102/00028312231208687
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized field experiments (96 studies in the 2020 WP; 89 RCT studies in the 2024 version per NSSA record)
population_location: PreK-12 students; tutoring programs in multiple countries (US-heavy, but the fetched text does not state a US share)
outcome: Learning outcomes (literacy and math assessments)
effect_as_reported: Pooled ES 0.37 SD (2020 WP); 0.288 SD (SE 0.029) in the 2024 published version (0.290 SD literacy, 0.268 SD math)
excerpt: We find that tutoring programs yield consistently substantial positive impacts on learning, with an overall pooled ES of 0.288 SD (SE = 0.029, p < 0.001). ESs tend to be largest for programs that use teachers or paraprofessionals as tutors
note: Both pooled numbers and all moderators (teacher/paraprofessional > nonprofessional/parent; earlier grades; during school > after school) confirmed; the WP abstract states the 0.37 SD and the moderator pattern verbatim. 2024 version also adds >=3 sessions/week as a moderator. "Mostly US" not confirmed in fetched text. Published 2024 text was read via the NSSA record (abstract), not the AERJ PDF itself.

correct_citation: Kim, J. S., & Quinn, D. M. (2013). The Effects of Summer Reading on Low-Income Children's Literacy Achievement From Kindergarten to Grade 8: A Meta-Analysis of Classroom and Home Interventions. Review of Educational Research, 83(3), 386-431. doi:10.3102/0034654313483906
design: Meta-analysis of 41 classroom- and home-based summer reading interventions (35 studies), 1998-2011
population_location: Children in kindergarten to grade 8, United States and Canada
outcome: Reading achievement (total, comprehension, fluency/decoding, vocabulary)
effect_as_reported: Grand mean d = .10 (95% CI .04-.15) on total reading; majority low-income samples: comprehension total d = .20, comprehension only d = .33; mixed-income comprehension total d = .00 (Qb p = .04); within-study sensitivity: low-income d = .14 vs mixed-income d = -.14
excerpt: intervention effects were positive and significant for majority low-income samples for total reading achievement (d = .10), reading comprehension total (d = .20), reading comprehension only (d = .33), and fluency and decoding combined (d = .23).
note: The d = .20 is for "reading comprehension total"; comprehension-only is d = .33 for majority low-income samples.

correct_citation: Herrera, C., Grossman, J. B., & Linden, L. L. (2013). Staying on Track: Testing Higher Achievement's Long-Term Impact on Academic Outcomes and High School Choice. New York: MDRC. (WWC Single Study Review, April 2014)
design: Randomized controlled trial (lottery), meets WWC standards without reservations
population_location: 952 incoming 5th and 6th graders (3 cohorts, 2006-2008) in Washington, DC and Alexandria, Virginia; analysis sample about 719-815
outcome: SAT-10 math problem solving and reading comprehension; high school choice
effect_as_reported: Year 4 math problem solving ES 0.11 (p < .05, improvement index +4); reading comprehension ES 0.04 (not significant)
excerpt: 4 years after randomization, students who were offered participation in Higher Achievement had significantly higher standardized test scores in mathematical problem solving.
note: n = 952 and math finding confirmed. Differs: sites were Washington, DC AND Alexandria, VA; the program is a multi-year summer and after-school program starting before grade 5 or 6. The null reading result is from this same study (year 4), not from a "later expansion study"; no expansion study is described in this source, so that part is unverified here.

correct_citation: Bowen, D. H., & Kisida, B. (2023). Investigating the Causal Effects of Arts Education. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 42(3), 624-647 (online 2022). doi:10.1002/pam.22449
design: Cluster randomized controlled trial, 42 elementary and middle schools

outcome: Disciplinary infractions, STAAR writing and other tests, survey-based engagement, college aspirations, empathy, tolerance
effect_as_reported: Disciplinary infractions -3.6 percentage points; writing +0.13 SD; emotional empathy +0.07 SD; elementary: significant gains in school engagement, college aspirations, cognitive empathy
excerpt: We find that arts learning reduces the proportion of students receiving disciplinary infractions by 3.6 percentage points, increases standardized writing achievement scores by 0.13 of a standard deviation

The "20.7 percent less likely" press figure was not found in any of the three press pages fetched (Chalkbeat, Hill Strategies, The 74 all report 3.6 percentage points).

correct_citation: Gray-Lobe, G., Pathak, P. A., & Walters, C. R. (2023). The Long-Term Effects of Universal Preschool in Boston. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 138(1), 363-411. doi:10.1093/qje/qjac036
design: Admission-lottery natural experiment (instrumental variables)
population_location: Applicants to Boston Public Schools public pre-K, Boston, Massachusetts
outcome: College enrollment, SAT taking, high school graduation, discipline, state achievement test scores
effect_as_reported: On-time college enrollment +8.3 percentage points (18% over 46% base); ever college +5.4 pp; HS graduation +6.0 pp; SAT taking +8.5 pp; no detectable effect on state achievement test scores
excerpt: Preschool enrollment boosts college attendance as well as SAT test taking and high school graduation. Preschool also decreases high school disciplinary measures including juvenile incarceration, but has no detectable effect on state achievement test scores.

correct_citation: Heller, S. B., Shah, A. K., Guryan, J., Ludwig, J., Mullainathan, S., & Pollack, H. A. (2017). Thinking, Fast and Slow? design: Three randomized controlled trials (two of Becoming a Man, 2009-10 and 2013-15; one in the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center)
population_location: Disadvantaged male Chicago Public Schools students, Chicago, Illinois
outcome: Arrests (total, violent), school engagement, high school graduation

excerpt: In the two studies participation in the program reduced total arrests during the intervention period by 28–35%, reduced violent-crime arrests by 45–50%, improved school engagement, and in the first study where we have follow-up data, increased graduation rates by 12–19%.
note: Resolves the source disagreement: graduation is measured in the FIRST study only (no post-program data for study 2). The 2013 WP19014 figure of 3-10 percentage points (7-22%) was a projection from schooling-index gains ("could lead to"), not a measured graduation effect. QJE volume/pages not re-fetched.

correct_citation: Hanselman, P., Rozek, C. S., Grigg, J., & Borman, G. D. (2017). New Evidence on Self-Affirmation Effects and Theorized Sources of Heterogeneity from Large-Scale Replications. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 405-424 (online 2016). doi:10.1037/edu0000141

correct_citation: Ballard, P. J., Hoyt, L. T., & Pachucki, M. C. (2019). Impacts of Adolescent and Young Adult Civic Engagement on Health and Socioeconomic Status in Adulthood. Child Development, 90(4), 1138-1154. doi:10.1111/cdev.12998

correct_citation: Lovenheim, M. F., Reback, R., & Wedenoja, L. (2016). How Does Access to Health Care Affect Teen Fertility and High School Dropout Rates? Evidence from School-based Health Centers. NBER Working Paper 22030. doi:10.3386/w22030

correct_citation: Sharkey, P. (2010). The acute effect of local homicides on children's cognitive performance. PNAS, 107(26), 11733-11738. doi:10.1073/pnas.1000690107
design: Natural experiment exploiting timing of homicides relative to assessment dates within neighborhoods (neighborhood fixed effects)
population_location: Children ages 5-17 in the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods, Chicago; replicated in the Three City Study Chicago sample
outcome: WISC-R vocabulary and WRAT3 reading assessments

correct_citation: Kemple, J. J., & Snipes, J. C. (2000). Career Academies: Impacts on Students' Engagement and Performance in High School. New York: Manpower Demonstration Research Corporation (MDRC). ERIC ED441075

correct_citation: Neild, R. C., & Balfanz, R. (2006). Unfulfilled Promise: The Dimensions and Characteristics of Philadelphia's Dropout Crisis, 2000-2005. Philadelphia Youth Network / Project U-Turn, Johns Hopkins University and University of Pennsylvania
design: Descriptive longitudinal cohort analysis of district administrative data
population_location: Philadelphia public school students, classes of 2000-2005
outcome: Graduation and dropout; early-warning predictors
effect_as_reported: Six-year graduation 54-58% (four-year 45-52%); 8th graders attending <80% had 78% dropout, failing math/English 77%; one 9th-grade flag gave >=75% probability of dropout; 80% of dropouts were at-risk 8th OR 9th graders
excerpt: Eighty percent of the students who dropped out of school were either at-risk 8th graders or at-risk 9th graders.
note: The 3-in-4 (>=75%) 8th-grade finding is confirmed. Differs: the 80% figure is for at-risk 8th graders and at-risk 9th graders combined, not the 9th-grade indicators alone. The report also says: "Two 8th grade factors gave students at least a 75% probability of dropping out of school" (attendance below 80%; failing math and/or English). "40% left without graduating" is the Fordham commentary's paraphrase; the report gives six-year graduation rates of 54-58%.

correct_citation: Bergman, P. (2021). Parent-Child Information Frictions and Human Capital Investment: Evidence from a Field Experiment. Journal of Political Economy, 129(1), 286-322. doi:10.1086/711410 (CESifo Working Paper 5391, 2015)
